title: The Spring Southwest Sold a Plane and Kept Its Timetable
dek: Short of cash in 1972, Southwest Airlines sold one of its four jets and asked its ground crews to fly the old schedule with three by turning planes in ten minutes.

story.founder: Lamar Muse and Bill Franklin (with co-founders Herb Kelleher and Rollin King)
story.event: Selling the fourth Boeing 737 and keeping the timetable with ten-minute turnarounds
story.summary: In the spring of 1972 Southwest Airlines, less than a year into flying and short of cash, sold the fourth of its four Boeing 737s on the decision of its president, Lamar Muse. To keep a timetable built for four aircraft, ground operations chief Bill Franklin had crews turn planes around at the gate in ten minutes, against thirty or more elsewhere, under threat of dismissal. The quick turn became the airline's signature, and Southwest made its first annual profit in 1973.
paragraphs: In the spring of 1972 Southwest Airlines had been flying for less than a year, and it was running out of money. Rollin King and Herb Kelleher had founded the company in 1967, and Kelleher, a lawyer, had led a three-year fight through the courts for its right to fly within Texas. In January 1971 they hired Lamar Muse, an accountant turned airline executive, to run it, and on 18 June 1971 Southwest began flying from Dallas Love Field to Houston and San Antonio.

That autumn it had added a fourth Boeing 737 to its first three, for a fuller timetable and for charter work. The losses went on. Muse, the president, decided to sell the fourth plane; the trade magazine Airways reports that it went to Frontier Airlines and that the money paid wages and other bills. The company's own history puts the gain on the sale at $500,000. That left a schedule built for four aircraft, including fourteen round trips a day between Dallas and Houston, and three planes to fly it.

Most airlines kept a plane at the gate for thirty minutes or more between flights. With three aircraft, Southwest's sums needed ten. In the company's telling, Bill Franklin, the vice-president in charge of ground operations, answered, "We can," and then, "And we will." He also told his staff that anyone who could not turn a plane in ten minutes would be fired and replaced. Dan Johnson, then a young agent in Houston, told NPR in 2015 that he remembered Franklin slamming his hand on the table as he said it.

The crews took ideas from motor-racing pit stops, the company says. Sandra Bogan, a flight attendant from the first day, told NPR that hostesses went row to row lifting down bags before the door opened. New passengers waited in line on the tarmac while crews unloaded rubbish and refuelled, pilots helped tidy the cabin, and planes pushed back while people were still finding seats. They did not always make ten minutes, but they made it often enough for it to become the airline's signature. Johnson called it "a real team effort." In 1973 Southwest made its first annual profit, and it stayed profitable for 47 years.

quote.text: When pure necessity drives man to his work it takes an accidental and contingent character, it becomes a mere makeshift arrangement; it is deserted and left in ruins when necessity changes its course. But when his work is the outcome of joy, the forms that it takes have the elements of immortality.
quote.source_title: Sadhana: The Realisation of Life, Project Gutenberg eBook #6842
quote.connection: Tagore says work driven by sheer necessity is a makeshift, abandoned once the need passes, and only work born of joy endures. The ten-minute turn was born of a cash crisis and a threat of the sack, yet it outlived both. Whether necessity or the crews' pleasure in the rush kept it alive, the record does not settle.

reflection: Southwest lost a plane and kept its timetable. The arithmetic was simple; the hard part was asking people on the ground to do in ten minutes what others took thirty to do, with their jobs on the line. Decades later, those who were there still remembered it as a team effort.

When you are short of something, money, people or hours, it is worth asking whether the plan has to shrink or only the way of doing it. And if you pass the pressure on, notice how. Fear can get a job done once. Whether it keeps getting done may depend on whether the people doing it find something in it of their own.
invitation: Pick one task that always seems to take longer than it should. Today, watch it once from start to finish, and write down the single step where everyone ends up waiting.

cross_checks.claim: In 1972, short of money, Southwest sold one of its four Boeing 737s
To keep the schedule with three planes, ground crews under Bill Franklin turned aircraft in ten minutes, under threat of dismissal

research_notes: Founders: the slate named Herb Kelleher and Rollin King, but the 1972 decision to sell the plane was Lamar Muse's as president (Southwest's own history) and the ten-minute turn is credited to Bill Franklin (NPR, Southwest) or, by the Handbook of Texas, to Muse; the story gives Muse the sale, Franklin the turn and King and Kelleher the founding and the court fight. Franklin's title: 'vice president of ground operations' (NPR) or 'Vice President of Terminal Operations' (Southwest), so the story says 'in charge of ground operations'. Reason for the sale: Southwest, NPR and Airways tie it to cash (Airways: payroll); AvGeekery ties it to a federal court ruling against interstate charters. The story says only that the losses went on and leaves the ruling here. Money figures conflict: Southwest's anniversary site says $143 was left in the bank in spring 1972, while the Handbook of Texas says $148 was in the bank in January 1971, which looks like the same anecdote at different dates, so no bank balance is given. Southwest's site and NPR imply losses of $1.6 million by the time of the sale, but Wikipedia, citing the annual reports, gives $3.8 million lost in 1971 and $1.6 million in 1972 as a whole, so no loss figure is given. The $500,000 gain is Southwest's own figure (Wikipedia says only 'a small gain') and is attributed to the company. The fourth plane arrived in September 1971 (Southwest) or October 1971 (Wikipedia), so the story says 'that autumn'; Wikipedia dates the sale to May 1972 and Southwest to the spring. Competitors' gate time: Southwest's site says most airlines took an hour; the Handbook of Texas says thirty minutes or more; the story uses the conservative thirty. Franklin's words: NPR's source calls 'We can, and we will' a legend, and Southwest presents it as said, so the story says 'in the company's telling'. The 47 years of profit is the Handbook of Texas's count as of January 2020. The Southwest 50 site is cited from its Wayback Machine copy because the live domain no longer serves it. Funding is 'mixed': a 1971 public share offering, private and venture investment, and 90 per cent aircraft financing (Handbook of Texas). Arc set to 'setback' rather than the slate's 'hard-responsibility', because the episode is a forced sale met by a change of method.
